headline: High: A can write and run code while B is documentation-only, creating default-path prompt, data, and compliance risks mainly from A’s filesystem/network reach.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can read/write the local filesystem and run shell/subprocesses, so malicious content in shared files could influence it. B is documentation-only with no filesystem, clipboard, or API surfaces, so there is no direct ingestion path from B back into A. The pairwise injection pathway is therefore limited and requires an unusual manual bridge.
conditions: IF the operator manually copies B-generated text into A’s prompts or files, injection becomes possible.
IF A is pointed at attacker-controlled local files, A may follow embedded instructions.
mitigations: Keep B as read-only reference material.
Do not paste untrusted text from files into A’s prompts.
Store A’s working files in a separate directory from any user-controlled content.
Review any file-fed prompt before execution.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for file-fed prompts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches configuration secrets and academic/research data, but B has no filesystem, network, or stdin/stdout surfaces, so it cannot exfiltrate or ingest those data by default. The main leakage path is operator-mediated transfer from A into B, which is not automatic. Because B is inert, the blast radius is small and manual.
conditions: IF the operator exports A’s files or secrets into another system, leakage can occur.
IF B is replaced with a runnable variant, the leakage profile changes materially.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared folders.
Rotate any secrets after testing A.
Use separate workspaces for A and B.
Audit A’s outputs before copying them elsewhere.
requires-engineering: enforce secret-scanning on A’s outputs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has shell, subprocess, filesystem write, and allowlisted egress; B has none of those capabilities. There is no overlapping write surface or shared mutable resource documented, so direct capability conflict is unlikely. Any conflict would require an external orchestrator to give B new powers, which is not shown here.
conditions: IF an orchestrator grants B write or network permissions, overlap could emerge.
IF both agents are mounted onto the same writable directory, contention becomes possible.
mitigations: Run B in documentation-only mode.
Keep A and B on separate directories.
Avoid sharing mutable git or database state.
Check orchestration configs for hidden shared mounts.
requires-engineering: add locking for any future shared resource.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate content from papers and APIs, and B is a reference-only cheatsheet that may be used as an authoritative source by a human or workflow. If A’s output is copied into B-driven documentation or decisions without verification, errors can cascade across work products. B does not verify A’s claims, so the interaction exists in default human-mediated workflows.
conditions: IF A’s generated text is reused as factual input for B-based documentation, errors can propagate.
IF the operator treats A’s outputs as verified facts, downstream mistakes increase.
mitigations: Require a human fact-check before reuse.
Mark A outputs as draft-only.
Cross-check claims against source papers.
Keep B as a reference, not an authority.
requires-engineering: add citation validation before publication.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles configuration secrets and may process academic/research data in a local development environment, while B is documentation-only and touches no data classes. The mismatch is mainly that A’s default workflow can expose secrets or research materials outside intended controls, whereas B adds no compensating controls. This is a compliance risk for A’s handling, not a residency issue for B.
conditions: IF A is run with real secrets instead of placeholders, compliance obligations apply.
IF research data includes regulated content, A’s local-dev handling may violate policy.
mitigations: Use placeholder secrets in development.
Separate regulated data from the course environment.
Review retention settings for logs and notebooks.
Restrict access to A’s workspace.
requires-engineering: implement policy checks for regulated data classes.
